summary: Complex cooperative tasks require coordinated multi-agent behavior. Offline generative policies learn expressive cooperative behaviors from trajectories but remain limited by fixed datasets. Online reinforcement learning can improve them through environment interaction. However, fine-tuning flow policies is difficult because action likelihoods are hard to compute. We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.
title: TeamFlowRL: Online Policy Optimization of Decentralized Flow Policies for Multi-Agent Coordination

summary: Large language models increasingly work as teams of agents, and a team is expected to solve problems beyond the reach of any single member. Most evaluations credit a team for outperforming a single agent, without accounting for the additional computation: a team may consume many times the tokens of one agent, and a plain vote over independent answers already explains most of the reported gain. Two questions therefore remain open: When does interaction itself make a group smarter, and can a group improve its next generation by learning from its own work? We answer both with the equal-budget ladder, which grades a group against independent agents at three levels: outperforming a single agent, a compute-matched majority vote, and compute-matched pass@n. On this ladder we define Recursive Collective Intelligence (RCI) as a group whose own output, without a teacher or external labels, makes its next generation smarter at equal cost. Three findings follow. First, interaction improves collective intelligence when it moves information across agents: forwarding split facts lifts groups above pass@n at three model scales, by about a third at 27B. Second, organization emerges spontaneously: identical 27B agents form hubs and improve accuracy by 18 percentage points; encoding their organization in a prompt enables them to reach level 3 at less than half the token budget in a descriptive comparison. Third, groups recursively improve themselves: Two label-free generations progressively climb the ladder, the second 9B generation surpassing both pass@$n$ and a control trained on base-model turns; on PlanBench, HiddenBench and Hanabi, each generation outperforms its predecessor on unseen problems for four to six generations. A group therefore outperforms its members when it forwards useful information more efficiently than it spends tokens on coordination, and learns to do so from its own work.
title: Recursive Collective Intelligence: Emergence on an Equal-Budget Ladder in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

summary: This Perspective introduces a claim-sensitive framework for evaluating evidential warrant in chemistry as computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and automated experimentation expand discovery workflows . Defining the chemical warrant gap as the mismatch between generating plausible candidates or predictions and the evidential strength required to justify corresponding chemical claims, the paper organizes assessment around five selectively activated dimensions material realization, chemical identity, evidential and measurement adequacy, mechanistic discrimination, and operational robustness and domain transferability alongside cross-cutting provenance and a distinct consideration of safety and sustainability for responsible application . The framework is operationalized through a five-step evaluation procedure and illustrated via a bounded analysis of Pd surface reconstruction as well as applications across molecular generation, materials discovery, and automated laboratories .
title: The chemical warrant gap: From predictive discovery to reliable chemical knowledge

summary: AffectFusion v1.0.0 is an open, PII-anonymized, zero-leakage multilingual multimodal benchmark dataset for text-and-emoji emotion recognition spanning English (ENG), Native Bengali (BN), and Romanized Banglish (BNG) across 9 fine-grained emotion classes: Joy, Neutral, Anger, Sadness, Surprise, Sarcasm, Fear, Disgust, and Anticipation. Key Dataset Properties: • Total Size: 30,000 dual-stream samples partitioned strictly 80/10/10 into train_24k (24,000 balanced rows; 2,666–2,667 per class), val_3k (3,000 100% real scraped rows), and test_3k (3,000 100% real scraped rows). • Zero-Leakage Guarantee: Deduplicated by normalized text MD5 hash across splits; strictly 0 augmented rows and 0 external dataset rows appear in val_3k or test_3k. • 5,000 Blinded Human-Verified Gold Annotations: Independently verified by two researchers with AI labels hidden (2,500 rows each), achieving 83.00% raw agreement and Cohen's κ = 0.8087 (ENG: 0.8129, BN: 0.8128, BNG: 0.7958). Upgrades test_3k to 100% human-verified gold (574 AI labels corrected) and val_3k to 66.7% gold (276 corrected). • Unified 25-Column Dual-Stream Schema: Provides separated text_stream, emoji_stream, Unicode CLDR demoji_text, and baseline_input alongside emoji density, punctuation cues, sarcasm emoji flags, and transparent provenance flags (is_augmented, is_external_train_only, is_human_verified). • Privacy-by-Design: Automated regex masking replaces all URLs (<URL>), user handles (<USER>), emails (<EMAIL>), and phone numbers (<PHONE>) prior to storage. • Reference Phase-I Benchmarks on 100% Gold test_3k (N = 3,000): CNN-BiLSTM (54.20% Acc, 0.5375 Macro-F1), XLM-R Text-Only (54.50% Acc, 0.5341 Macro-F1), and XLM-R Early Fusion (64.07% Acc, 0.6366 Macro-F1; +13.17% Macro-F1 gain on emoji-bearing posts, paired t = 11.24, McNemar χ² = 117.86, p < 0.0001). Companion source code, Colab notebooks, and evaluation scripts are available at: https://github.com/ragibcs/AffectFusion

summary: TAL is a high-performance desktop application for crystallographic visualization and analysis, written in .NET 8 with MonoGame. It provides an interactive 3D environment for exploring crystal structures, intermolecular interactions, and advanced computational analyses, with particular strength in the precise detection and characterization of voids and cavities in molecular crystals. Purpose TAL is designed for researchers working with single-crystal X-ray diffraction data. It enables loading, visualization, and quantitative analysis of crystal structures, supporting studies of packing, porosity, host–guest chemistry, hydrogen bonding, and related phenomena. A core focus is accurate mapping of free space (cavities and channels) that accounts for both geometric packing and thermal motion. Key capabilities Structure loading and export : CIF (multi-block), SHELX RES/INS, XYZ, PDB, MOL/SDF, MOL2, Gaussian input, and CRYSTAL17 (.d12). Full write support for most formats, including proper handling of symmetry, ADP tensors, and space-group settings. Visualization : CPK, sticks, balls-and-sticks, ORTEP-style thermal ellipsoids, and coordination polyhedra. Multiple coloring schemes (element, symmetry, molecule, charge, hydrophobicity). Labels, short contacts, hydrogen bonds, unit cell, planes, and symmetry elements (ITA-style axes, planes, and centers). Hydrogen handling : Neutron-standard X–H distance normalization (manual and automatic pathways) and AFIX-aware Uiso recalculation for SHELX files. Cavity and porosity analysis (flagship feature): Signed-distance-function (SDF) voxel grid with flood-fill isolation of buried voids. Anisotropic treatment of atomic displacement parameters (ADPs): cavities are defined against 1σ thermal ellipsoids rather than spheres; symmetry-equivalent atoms carry correctly rotated ADP tensors. VdW radius scaling sweeps with derived QSPR descriptors (fragmentation index, collapse scale, electrostatic/hydrophobic frustration, etc.). Channel pathfinding, sphere-fit packing analysis, gas/solvent compatibility scoring, and detailed single-run or multi-scale reports. Explicit erosion model relating void volume loss to characteristic length (V/S) and thermal amplitude. Additional analysis tools : Hirshfeld surfaces, powder diffraction simulation (Cromer–Mann form factors), mean planes and Miller planes, morphology, structure overlay, H-bond graph-set topology, partial charges (PEOE/SQE), and hydrophobicity. Publication and interoperability : High-resolution screenshots, POV-Ray export of the full scene (atoms, bonds, cavities, planes, polyhedra), and CRYSTAL17 input generation with automatic standard-setting transformation. Implementation notes The cavity engine is deliberately exact rather than approximate: effective radii incorporate VdW multipliers and probe radius; ADP contributions are the physical 1σ half-axes; symmetry operations fully transform both positions and tensors (no diagonal-only shortcuts). Memory and resolution safeguards, smoothing options, and per-cavity visibility controls are included. All major analysis paths produce self-contained textual (and, where relevant, HTML) reports containing parameters, crystal data, and derived metrics. Technical summary Language / framework: C# / .NET 8, MonoGame, DockPanel Suite. Author: Daniel M. Kamiński, Lublin, Poland. License: Academic / non-commercial (see included LICENSE.txt); commercial licensing available on request. Home page: dkami.umcs.pl/tal Source code: https://github.com/DanielKami/Tal Keywords : crystallography, crystal structure visualization, cavity detection, voids, porosity, Hirshfeld surface, ORTEP, thermal ellipsoids, hydrogen bonds, powder diffraction, space-group transformation, .NET, MonoGame.   First citation:  Structural phase evolution in lupeol synthesis from betulin: solid-solution crystals, an isostructural aldehyde, and various derivative architectures CrystEngComm 2026 | Journal article

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Fifty entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature, among them: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7; a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients; a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset; a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten; a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998); a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation; a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight; a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. Light through a Jerlov water type. The package: computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963); converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors; gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m, and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers; integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth; gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two; and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent; ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum; carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models; converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient. Measurements it carries. Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type, against which the depth profile is checked; Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille; the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures; Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters; five published spectra of the absorption of pure water, Pope & Fry (1997), Smith & Baker (1981), Mason, Cone & Fry (2016), Lee et al. (2015) and Morel et al. (2007), for the caller to choose from; the eight stations of the clearest ocean water measured, Morel et al. (2007); the measured reflectance of ten materials found in and around water, from the USGS Spectral Library Version 7, for reference images of how they look through each water type. Without a water type. It gives: Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001, and the earlier edition of Morel 1988), or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013); the attenuation of the visible and of the whole shortwave from the surface to a depth, and the depth where a given fraction of the visible light is left, the euphotic depth among them, from the absorption and backscattering coefficients at 490 nm and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2007); from chlorophyll, the absorption by phytoplankton (Bricaud et al. 1995) and the b

summary: Nobody has blamed AI for November’s outages, but it did get me thinking. In a single week in November 2026, major incidents affecting Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, and Apple were attributed to a latent defect, a router replacement, a software bug, and an internal update, respectively. None of these incidents has been linked to AI-generated code. This paper explores what a failure caused by AI-written code with inadequate oversight might look like. Drawing on recent empirical studies and documented incidents, it presents five illustrative scenarios: a defect that passes self-written tests and remains dormant; a configuration change that precisely follows instructions; an agent fix that exacerbates the problem; a silent failure that falsely reports success; and a flaw that propagates as agents copy surrounding code. Each would pass the checks organizations typically rely on and would be described in terms similar to the November outages, without reference to AI, because code provenance is rarely documented. Evidence from Google indicates that robust review can mitigate the risk, although this capacity is expensive. The paper concludes with controls for each scenario and three AI-specific practices: recording provenance, limiting agent change size, and tiering agent permissions. AI assistance.  The author conceived, directed the investigation, drafted, and revised the article. AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Grammarly for editing) supported the literature search, iterative copyediting and revisions, and adversarial review. The author verified all sources and figures and is responsible for the content. Disclaimer. Views are the author’s own and do not represent Purdue University.

In a single week in November 2026, major incidents affecting Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, and Apple were attributed to a latent defect, a router replacement, a software bug, and an internal update, respectively. None of these incidents has been linked to AI-generated code. This paper explores what a failure caused by AI-written code with inadequate oversight might look like. Drawing on recent empirical studies and documented incidents, it presents five illustrative scenarios: a defect that passes self-written tests and remains dormant; a configuration change that precisely follows instructions; an agent fix that exacerbates the problem; a silent failure that falsely reports success; and a flaw that propagates as agents copy surrounding code. Each would pass the checks organizations typically rely on and would be described in terms similar to the November outages, without reference to AI, because code provenance is rarely documented. Evidence from Google indicates that robust review can mitigate the risk, although this capacity is expensive. The paper concludes with controls for each scenario and three AI-specific practices: recording provenance, limiting agent change size, and tiering agent permissions. AI assistance.  The author conceived, directed the investigation, drafted, and revised the article. AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and Grammarly for editing) supported the literature search, iterative copyediting and revisions, and adversarial review. The author verified all sources and figures and is responsible for the content. Disclaimer. Views are the author’s own and do not represent Purdue University.

summary: High-performance geospatial analysis library, CLI and dynamic tile server in Rust: 127 algorithms (56 also available in the browser via WebAssembly), streaming I/O for arbitrarily large DEMs, native CRS reprojection, windowed GeoTIFF and Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF reads (including ZSTD, band-interleaved, bottom-up and BigTIFF files such as the AlphaEarth Foundations embedding tiles), a native ECW decoder, an end-to-end satellite composite pipeline, foundation-model embeddings as first-class rasters (similarity maps, PCA false colour), embedded verifiable provenance in every output with a bit-exact determinism contract, and SurtGIS Server (`surtgis serve`), an analysis-first XYZ tile server with materialisation jobs where terrain operators, spectral formulas and embedding operators are tile-URL parameters. Covers terrain analysis, hydrology and remote sensing from a single dependency-free binary. This record archives the source of release v1.9.0.
title: SurtGIS: a high-performance raster geospatial analysis library, CLI and dynamic tile server in Rust

summary: Second pre-release of REAP. It adds the pieces for checking REAP on held-out documents, choosing K and map settings with every choice declared, and placing new passages into an existing map. Install from this tag (REAP isn't on PyPI yet): pip install "reap-topics[projection] @ git+https://github.com/Thru-Echoes/REAP@v0.2.0" New reap.holdout : hold-out comparison harness, with parametric UMAP and identity baselines. reap.selection : choose K and UMAP settings with every choice declared and no defaults. reap.placement : four projection heads (REAP's MLP, a scaled MLP, ridge, nearest-neighbour), held-out placement of reference passages, and a calibrated inside test. Versioned result record files ( reap.repro_bundle ). Snapshots for the earnings-call and presidential-speech corpus, and raw Korean-forest pledge embeddings. Drivers for hold-out cells and their fail-closed aggregation, and a driver that maps a reference set and projects other document sets into it. Parameter-search records: the benchmark and reference drivers refuse to run without one, so default settings can't be mistaken for results. Fixed train_projection_head no longer stops when the training rows leave a last batch of one row. The README and CONTRIBUTING install and clone commands now work. Full list in CHANGELOG.md .
title: REAP: Reproducible Embeddings via Averaged Projection

Install from this tag (REAP isn't on PyPI yet): pip install "reap-topics[projection] @ git+https://github.com/Thru-Echoes/REAP@v0.2.0" New reap.holdout : hold-out comparison harness, with parametric UMAP and identity baselines. reap.selection : choose K and UMAP settings with every choice declared and no defaults. reap.placement : four projection heads (REAP's MLP, a scaled MLP, ridge, nearest-neighbour), held-out placement of reference passages, and a calibrated inside test. Versioned result record files ( reap.repro_bundle ). Snapshots for the earnings-call and presidential-speech corpus, and raw Korean-forest pledge embeddings. Drivers for hold-out cells and their fail-closed aggregation, and a driver that maps a reference set and projects other document sets into it. Parameter-search records: the benchmark and reference drivers refuse to run without one, so default settings can't be mistaken for results. Fixed train_projection_head no longer stops when the training rows leave a last batch of one row. The README and CONTRIBUTING install and clone commands now work. Full list in CHANGELOG.md .
